newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel hears data on infant formula additives.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel hears data on infant formula additives.

text.p: Scientists and manufacturers told federal health advisers Wednesday that two nutrients should be added to premature infant formula.

The panel, convened by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to consider if the agency should mandate inclusion in premature infant formula of docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and arachidonic acid (ARA), known as long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids, is due to report to the FDA in the fall.
If the panel backs addition of DHA and ARA, it would be a boost to Columbia, Md.-based Martek Biosciences Corp.

Martek is one of the world's largest producers of DHA, a major building block of brain and eye tissue. Martek says 60 percent of brain tissue is made up of fat, and almost half of that is composed of DHA. The firm produces ARA as well, also an essential fatty acid.
Other manufacturers at the meeting, including Hoffmann-La Roche and Nestle, argued for inclusion of DHA and ARA.
Representatives of Abbott Laboratories' Ross Labs division said the substances should not be added until further safety studies were completed. Ross has not licensed Martek's DHA.

Infant formulas sold in the U.S. have remain essentially unchanged since 1985, although manufacturers of pre-term formula have periodically added ingredients if they were able to convince the FDA the additions were safe.
The agency is considering mandating formula ingredients, but is waiting for the advisers' conclusions.

Even without the panel's backing, formula manufacturers can petition the FDA to add the ingredients, based primarily on safety data. Safety of DHA sources -- fish, microalgae, and fungi -- however, has been a concern of the agency and of some in the scientific community.
DHA and ARA are found naturally in mother's milk, and are already incorporated into formulas for premature babies in several countries, including the United Kingdom.
A World Health Organization panel has recommended that all infant formula be enriched with the substances.

Several published studies, plus data presented at the meeting, indicate that DHA and ARA added to formula helps improve visual acuity and speeds brain development in premature infants. Babies born early miss placental transmission of DHA and ARA because most of it is accumulated during the third trimester. Breast milk is not always available in women who have given birth prematurely.
Despite evidence for efficacy, there has been concern that some DHA -- that derived from fish -- might actually retard infants' growth.
